newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish coalition likely to solve tax row.
newsitem.headline: Polish coalition likely to solve tax row.

text.p: The two parties in Poland's ruling leftist coalition appeared set on Friday to settle their dispute over next year's taxes, which threatened to throw the country's finances into disarray.

The Polish Peasant Party, the coalition's smaller group, suggested it might back out of its support for a provision slashing personal income tax for the lowest-paid, which could undermine the government's nearly-complete budget draft.
Peasants' deputy leader Andrzej Benktowski told PAP news agency his party might agree that the regulation, approved by the lower house of parliament on Thursday, should be blocked in the senate.

The Peasants on Thursday unexpectedly joined forces with the opposition against its coalition partner, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), to introduce a new lower tax band at 17 percent.

In a shock defeat for the government, the chamber approved a bill setting next year's tax levels at 17, 20, 33 and 45 percent from the current 21, 33 and 45 percent despite finance ministry warnings that the move would cost the budget about 4.6 billion zlotys ($1.63 billion) in lost revenues.

The ministry said lower revenues would have to be compensated either by radical curbs in spending or by boosting next year's budget deficit, which is now planned at 2.8 percent of gross domestic product, the same level as in 1996.

The central bank said on Thursday that even the 2.8-percent deficit would require a more restrictive monetary policy next year to achieve the government's target to cut year-on-year inflation to 13 percent in December 1997 from September's 19.5.

The government, debating final details of its budget draft on Friday before submitting it to parliament next week, is likely to proceed as if the lower house's tax decision had never happened, a source close to the cabinet said.
The source, who asked not to be named, told Reuters the budget draft would be based on a three-level tax scale because it is legally binding at the moment.

The government and the SLD want to reduce next year's personal tax levels to 20, 31 and 45 percent, which would cost the budget only about two billion zlotys -- a sum which would not threaten the budget, according to the finance ministry.

SLD leader Jozef Oleksy said his party would do all it could to enforce the three levels in the senate, which is due to begin a two-day meeting on October 30. The government has until October 31 to present its budget draft to parliament.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski, whose veto may block any bill as a last resort, has criticised the 17 percent tax rate.

PAP quoted Bentkowski as saying that his party might agree to approve the three levels in the senate if Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko presented detailed data showing that the 17 percent tax level was not economically viable.
"A decision (on the tax cut) was made according to the full knowledge we had at that time," he said.
He added that his party supported the 17 percent tax because it had reason to believe Kolodko had not revealed all possible budget revenues.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz earlier said that by voting in favour of the tax the Peasants and other parties had wanted to boost their popularity ahead of next year's general elections at the expense of the economy. ($1=2.8180 Zloty)
